seo.title: Private Cinemas | DAVG
seo.description: Seat positions determine sightlines, screen size, speaker geometry, and much of the room design. Equipment comes after that plan.

hero.heading: Start with the seats. Build the room around them.
hero.deck: Seat positions determine sightlines, screen size, speaker geometry, and much of the room design. Equipment comes after that plan.

study: One conceptual cinema section and a separate wall diagram. Neither is a measured room.

chapters.title: Does this need to be a dedicated cinema?
paragraphs: A dedicated room lets you control light, seating and sound more closely. A shared media room has to accommodate daylight, circulation and other uses.
Decide how the room will be used and how often. A cinema is justified by that use, not by filling a spare room with the largest possible screen.
The room dimensions and structure create limits before a projector is selected. Doors, soffits, ceiling height and equipment access all belong in the first survey.
chapters.visual: One measured or clearly illustrative room cutaway with doors, soffits and intended seat rows.

chapters.title: The second row needs a sightline too.
paragraphs: Screen height and seat distance determine how comfortably people can watch. A rear row needs to see over the front row without forcing the screen too high.
Reclining seats change clearances and eye positions. Riser height follows those positions and the room’s available headroom.
Review the plan and section together. The last seat should be part of the design from the start, not added after the screen is ordered.
chapters.visual: Section drawing showing actual eye positions and sightlines. No universal seat-distance or riser rule.

chapters.title: Projection or direct view?
paragraphs: Projection can create a large image with equipment outside the screen plane. It also depends on throw distance, screen material, light control and projector placement.
A direct-view display brings its own light source to the screen. Its size, installation access, reflections and wall construction still need review.

An acoustically transparent projection screen allows suitable speakers behind it. Screen material must fit the projector geometry and lighting conditions; an ambient-light-rejecting label is not a cure for every room.
chapters.visual: Show projector/light path and speakers behind an AT screen. Pair with a direct-view wall section.

rows: Large image and flexible screen integration
Throw, room light, ventilation and material

chapters.title: Channels describe positions, not quality.
paragraphs: A 7.2.4 installation describes seven main-channel speaker positions, two subwoofers in the design, and four height-channel positions. The source format’s LFE channel and the number of installed subwoofers are different things.
Ear-level speakers establish the horizontal sound field. Overhead speakers provide the height layer; placing both groups in the ceiling weakens that separation.
Subwoofer positions and calibration affect how evenly bass reaches the seats. Additional speakers or subwoofers should solve a defined coverage problem.
chapters.visual: Plan and section of the same room with separate ear-level, height and subwoofer labels. Do not call any existing DAVG project 7.2.4 without records.

chapters.title: Treating the room and isolating it are different work.
paragraphs: Acoustic treatment changes reflections and decay inside the room. Sound isolation reduces transmission through the room’s boundaries.
Isolation depends on walls, ceilings, doors, penetrations and paths around them. A treated wall does not stop sound escaping through an untreated door or duct.
Ventilation has to move air without creating an obvious noise or sound path. That coordination belongs with the builder and mechanical team before the finish package is set.
chapters.visual: Real assembly sections, door seal and ventilation path. Clearly label design concepts; no unverified decibel claims.

chapters.title: Make the room ready in one deliberate sequence.
paragraphs: A movie scene can select the source, set the sound path, lower supported shades and fade lights to their agreed levels. A Pause scene can bring enough light back to move around.
Commissioning checks the image, sound, sources and controls at the intended seats. The target is a consistent experience across the designed seating area.
Leave access for projector filters, equipment replacement and cable service. The room should remain serviceable after the decorative panels are installed.
chapters.visual: Movie and Pause states of the same room, with a labeled service-access elevation.

projectPaths.title: Assess the available room
projectPaths.body: Measure structure, doors, seating and noise paths. Decide what can be improved within the existing envelope and what requires construction.

projectPaths.title: Use access to solve the room
projectPaths.body: Coordinate risers, isolation details, ventilation, wiring and screen wall before finishing. Review sightlines with the selected seating.

projectPaths.title: Reserve the right envelope
projectPaths.body: Coordinate dimensions, structure, mechanical noise, equipment access and adjoining rooms with the architect and builder. Allow the cinema design to shape the shell early.

scopeOptions.label: Good — dedicated viewing
scopeOptions.scope: Defined seating plan, suitable image and sound, basic light control and commissioned operation.
scopeOptions.dependencies: Existing envelope limits and required construction are explicit.

scopeOptions.label: Better — designed cinema
scopeOptions.scope: Coordinated sightlines, screen/speaker geometry, subwoofer placement, acoustic treatment and scene control.
scopeOptions.dependencies: Isolation work is a separate assembly scope, not implied by treatment.

scopeOptions.label: Best — room and structure together
scopeOptions.scope: Early architectural coordination, detailed isolation/ventilation design, custom integration and documented commissioning.
scopeOptions.dependencies: Channel count and equipment choices follow the room; no automatic hardware ladder.

faqs.question: How big does the room need to be?
faqs.answer: Enough for the chosen seats, clearances, image and speaker geometry. A measured plan determines the usable layout; one minimum dimension does not describe every cinema.

faqs.question: Will acoustic panels keep sound upstairs quiet?
faqs.answer: Panels mainly change sound inside the cinema. Reducing transmission upstairs requires a review of structure, boundaries and flanking paths.

faqs.question: Is more Atmos always better?
faqs.answer: No. Each channel needs a useful position and appropriate coverage; the room and seats determine whether more channels help.

faqs.question: What drives cost?
faqs.answer: Construction, seating, screen and projector/display, speaker system, acoustic work, isolation, ventilation and commissioning.

inquiry.body: Tell us which rooms matter, what already exists, and when construction starts. Share plans or photographs if you have them.

openingQA.question: What makes a room work as a cinema?
answer: Seat positions establish sightlines and speaker geometry. The screen, lighting, acoustic treatment and ventilation then need to support those positions.
A coordinated room design addresses the experience at the intended seats. Adding larger equipment alone does not resolve the room.
